In 2022, HelloFresh had 4 ML models running in production across the business. By the time I moved on, there were 70. The platform those models ran on generated $25M+ in annual revenue, reached 400x MAU growth, and cut the average time-to-production for a new model from 3 months to 1 month.

I was the Staff PM responsible for the AI/ML Platform the whole time. I want to write down what actually drove those results — not the headline numbers, but the operational decisions behind them.

---

## Why most AI platforms stall at "proof of concept"

The 4-model state we started from wasn't the result of talent gaps or lack of ambition. HelloFresh had excellent data scientists. The constraint was infrastructure and process, not people.

Every model was its own island. Each team had built their own:
- Feature pipelines
- Training infrastructure
- Deployment process
- Monitoring (or lack of it)

When something broke — and it always breaks — the only person who could fix it was the person who built it. No shared vocabulary, no shared tooling, no shared standards. Knowledge lived in heads and Confluence pages nobody read.

The first thing I learned: **the bottleneck in AI at scale is almost never the model. It's the scaffold around it.**

### 2. Operational Readiness Checklists (ORC)

Before a model could go to production, it had to pass a checklist. Not a bureaucratic checklist — a functional one. Questions like:

- What's the fallback behavior when the model call times out?
- Who owns the model drift alert at 2am?
- What's the business impact of a false positive vs. false negative, and have you validated the threshold against it?

## The number that matters

The metric I'm most proud of isn't the 70 models. It's the 1 month.

When I started, it took 3 months from "model trained and validated" to "model generating revenue in production." By the time we finished, it was 1 month. That's not a small improvement — it's the difference between data science teams being a competitive advantage and being a lagging indicator.
